item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Unlike many cases of not-up-to-modern-standards tone, I don't think this one needs updating.
Don't get me wrong, there are several elements that wouldn't fly if posted today. The awkward -02 designation being the biggest in my eyes.
But those don't make me cringe, get in the way of understanding what's going on, or overturn my suspension of disbelief that this is an official scientific write-up.

My headcanon is that this is a file from the in-universe early days of The Foundation. A bit of semi-obsolete documentation that doesn't meet current protocol, but is deemed unlikely to cause issues so is low down on the list of priorities for records overhaul.

item.title: Re: Possible solution...
item.content:encoded:
So many reasons, but I'm going to focus on two:
First, it would be a cross-test between SCPs. We don't know what would happen.
Second, with limited exceptions, the Foundation tends not to use these objects.

item.content:encoded:
I strongly feel that this is a Euclid-class, not safe. Sure, it's contained and as long as we don't take it out of its flame-retardant vacuum box it can't hurt us. 2 things: First, the definition for Euclid on How to Write an SCP is that it "<snip>require[s] fairly specific containment procedures, but if they're followed, the object's easily contained". Second, how do we know there aren't more of these out there?

E: Nonetheless, upvoted.

item.content:encoded:
…it would be interesting to have a heat measure too. Plus I second Dr Nostrand, that last period sounds bad to me. However:

Experiments have shown that the fire will continue to burn even:

  • In a vacuum
  • Under water
  • In a nitrogen-saturated environment
  • Under intense airflow
  • In a refrigerated environment
  • Encased in a fire-retardant covering

And this, kids, explains how can Spongebob manage to make bonefires.

item.title: Any pedants here?
item.content:encoded:
The involvement of that organization may go some way to explaining why SCP-310 was located where it was, what it had been used for, and what it started the blaze that lead to its recovery by the Foundation. However, the question of SCP-310's origin is still open.

This doesn't make any sense to me, grammatically. Is the author trying to ask the question of what was ignited or what event caused the blaze that led to the recovery? Maybe it's "what had started the blaze." That reads a bit dumb though, because SCP-310 obviously started the blaze.

item.title: Maybe I'm missing something
item.content:encoded: Why does it burn skin/flesh? I imagine something with as much water as a human isn't semi-flammable. Obviously the clothing burns, and that hurts, but why would it spread to thebody?

item.title: Possibly incorrect?
item.content:encoded:
Any object ignited by SCP-310 are designated SCP-310-02 and are classified Euclid until fully consumed, whereupon they revert to Safe classification.

Wouldn't they then be reverted to "Neutralized" if they were fully consumed?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
It seems to me that this SCP is potentially Keter class (except that it's not actively hostile/sentient), unless I misunderstand it. Which I must, now that I think of it - it seems that the initial circumstances of its acquisition would have led to a potential extinction event, in that a burning house would almost certainly spark downstream fires. Since even semi-flammable materials (anything with carbon, I'd imagine) are vulnerable, all it would take is spreading to nearby grass to have an unquenchable conflagration. Although it could be contained by trenching, I suppose. Maybe not Keter after all.

Very interesting! Thank you.
